title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: After thanking Anna Pavlovna for her delightful evening, the guests began to leave.

Pierre was an awkward man. Heavyset, about average height, broad-shouldered, with enormous red hands, he had no idea — as people say — how to enter a drawing room and even less how to exit one gracefully. He was also hopelessly absent-minded. When he stood to go, he picked up the general's three-cornered hat instead of his own and stood there tugging at its plume until the general asked for it back. All of this clumsiness was redeemed, however, by his kind, simple, and genuinely modest expression. Anna Pavlovna turned to him with a Christian gentleness that conveyed forgiveness for his blunders, nodded, and said: "I hope to see you again, but I also hope you'll change your opinions, my dear Monsieur Pierre."

He made no reply and only bowed, but once again everyone noticed that smile of his — a smile that said nothing at all, except perhaps: "Opinions are opinions, but can't you see what a decent, good-natured fellow I am?" And everyone, including Anna Pavlovna, could feel this.

Prince Andrew had gone out into the hall and, with his shoulders turned to the footman helping him on with his cloak, listened with cold indifference to his wife chattering with Prince Hippolyte, who had also come out. Prince Hippolyte stood close to the pretty, pregnant princess, staring at her through his monocle.
[Speaking in French] "Go inside, Annette, or you'll catch cold," said the little princess, taking leave of Anna Pavlovna. "It's settled," she added in a low voice.
Anna Pavlovna had already managed to speak with Lise about the match she was arranging between Anatole and the little princess's sister-in-law.
"I'm counting on you, my dear," said Anna Pavlovna, also speaking softly. "Write to her and let me know what her father thinks of it. Goodbye!" And she went back inside.
Prince Hippolyte walked up to the little princess and, leaning his face close to hers, began whispering something.

Two footmen — the princess's and his own — stood holding a shawl and a cloak, waiting for the conversation to end. They listened to the French being spoken, which meant nothing to them, with an expression that suggested they understood perfectly well but were too polite to show it. The princess, as always, spoke with a smile and listened with a laugh.
"I'm so glad I didn't go to the ambassador's," said Prince Hippolyte. "So dull. It's been a delightful evening, hasn't it? Delightful!"
"They say the ball will be wonderful," the princess replied, drawing up her soft little lip. "All the prettiest women in society will be there."

"Not all — because you won't be there. Not all," said Prince Hippolyte with a joyful smile. And snatching the shawl from the footman — even pushing the man aside — he began wrapping it around the princess. Whether from clumsiness or by design (no one could tell which), after adjusting the shawl he kept his arm around her for a long time, as though embracing her.
Still smiling, she moved gracefully away, turning to glance at her husband. Prince Andrew's eyes were closed — he looked utterly weary and sleepy.
"Ready?" he asked his wife, looking past her.

Prince Hippolyte hurriedly threw on his cloak, which in the latest fashion reached all the way to his heels, and stumbling in it, ran out to the porch after the princess, whom a footman was helping into the carriage.
[Speaking in French] "Princess, goodbye!" he cried, stumbling over his words as much as his feet.
The princess, gathering up her skirt, was taking her seat in the dark carriage. Her husband was adjusting his saber. Prince Hippolyte, under the pretense of helping, was getting in everyone's way.
"Step aside, sir," said Prince Andrew in Russian, his tone cold and unpleasant, to Prince Hippolyte who was blocking his path.
"I'm expecting you, Pierre," said the same voice, but now gentle and affectionate.
The driver started and the carriage wheels clattered. Prince Hippolyte stood in the porch laughing convulsively as he waited for the vicomte, whom he had promised to take home.

[Speaking in French] "Well, my friend," said the vicomte, settling himself beside Hippolyte in the carriage, "your little princess is very charming, very charming indeed — quite French." And he kissed his fingertips. Hippolyte burst out laughing.
"You know, for all your innocent airs you're quite the rascal," the vicomte continued. "I pity the poor husband — that little officer who puts on the airs of a king."
Hippolyte spluttered with laughter again. "And you were saying Russian ladies can't compare with the French? You just have to know how to handle them."

Pierre arrived at the house first and went into Prince Andrew's study as if he owned the place. Out of habit he immediately flopped down on the sofa, grabbed the first book his hand found on the shelf — it happened to be Caesar's Commentaries — and, propping himself on his elbow, began reading from the middle.
"What have you done to Mademoiselle Scherer? She's going to be quite ill after that," said Prince Andrew as he came into the study, rubbing his small white hands.
Pierre rolled his whole body over, making the sofa creak. He turned his eager face toward Prince Andrew, smiled, and waved his hand.
"That abbé is very interesting, but he's got it all wrong. In my opinion, perpetual peace is possible, but — how do I put it — not through a balance of political power..."
It was obvious that Prince Andrew had no interest in this kind of abstract discussion.
"You can't go around saying everything you think, my friend. Anyway, have you finally decided on anything? Are you going to be a guardsman or a diplomat?" asked Prince Andrew after a brief silence.
Pierre sat up on the sofa with his legs tucked under him.
"Honestly, I still don't know. I don't like either option."
"But you have to choose something! Your father expects it."

Pierre had been sent abroad at the age of ten with a tutor — an abbé — and had stayed away until he was twenty. When he returned to Moscow, his father dismissed the tutor and told the young man: "Now go to Petersburg, look around, and choose a career. I'll agree to anything. Here's a letter to Prince Vasili, and here's money. Write and tell me everything, and I'll help you however I can." Pierre had been trying to choose a career for three months now and had settled on nothing. It was this choice that Prince Andrew was asking about. Pierre rubbed his forehead.
"But he must be a Freemason," he said, referring to the abbé he had met that evening.
"That's all nonsense," Prince Andrew interrupted again. "Let's talk about something real. Have you been to the Horse Guards?"

"No, I haven't. But here's what I've been thinking, and I wanted to tell you: there's a war on against Napoleon. If it were a war for freedom, I'd understand it and I'd be the first to enlist. But to help England and Austria against the greatest man in the world — that's not right."

Prince Andrew merely shrugged at Pierre's naive words. He put on the look of a man who finds it pointless to reply to such nonsense, though in truth it would have been hard to give any better answer than the one he gave to this simplistic question.
"If nobody fought except from personal conviction, there would be no wars," he said.
"And that would be wonderful," said Pierre.
Prince Andrew smiled with irony.
"Very likely it would be wonderful, but it will never happen."
"Well then, why are you going to war?" asked Pierre.
"Why? I don't know. I have to. Besides, I'm going..." He paused. "I'm going because the life I'm leading here doesn't suit me!"

title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: The gray-haired valet sat drowsily listening to the prince snoring in his large study. From the far side of the house, through closed doors, came the sound of a difficult passage from a Dussek sonata—repeated twenty times over.

Just then, a closed carriage and a hooded cart pulled up to the front porch. Prince Andrei stepped out, helped his small wife down, and let her enter the house ahead of him. Old Tikhon, wearing a wig, poked his head out of the antechamber door, whispered that the prince was sleeping, and quickly shut it again. Tikhon knew that neither the son's arrival nor any other unusual event was allowed to disturb the appointed order of the day. Prince Andrei apparently knew this just as well as Tikhon. He checked his watch, as if to confirm whether his father's habits had changed since his last visit, and, satisfied that they hadn't, turned to his wife.
"He won't be up for twenty minutes. Let's go see Mary," he said.
The little princess had put on weight since they'd last been here, but her eyes and her short, downy upper lip—which lifted when she began to speak—were as merry and charming as ever.

"Why, this is a palace!" she said to her husband, looking around with the expression people use when complimenting their host at a ball. "Come on, quick, quick!" And she flashed a smile at Tikhon, at her husband, and at the footman escorting them.
"Is that Mary practicing? Let's sneak up and surprise her."
Prince Andrei followed her with a courteous but melancholy expression.
"You've gotten older, Tikhon," he said in passing to the old man, who kissed his hand.
Before they reached the room from which the clavichord music was coming, the pretty, fair-haired Frenchwoman, Mademoiselle Bourienne, burst out, apparently beside herself with excitement.
"Oh, what joy for the princess!" she cried. "At last! I must go tell her!"
"No, no, please don't... You're Mademoiselle Bourienne," said the little princess, kissing her. "I feel like I already know you through my sister-in-law's friendship. She wasn't expecting us?"
They approached the sitting room door, from which the same passage of the sonata could be heard repeating. Prince Andrei stopped and made a pained face, as if bracing for something unpleasant.

The little princess walked in. The music broke off mid-phrase, a cry rang out, followed by Princess Mary's heavy footsteps and the sound of kissing. When Prince Andrei entered, the two princesses—who had met only once before, briefly, at his wedding—were locked in each other's arms, pressing their lips to whatever part of each other's face they could reach. Mademoiselle Bourienne stood nearby with her hand pressed to her heart, wearing a blissful smile and looking equally prepared to burst into tears or laughter. Prince Andrei shrugged and frowned, the way music lovers do when they hear a wrong note. The two women released each other, then immediately seized each other's hands again, kissing them, pulling them away, and kissing each other's faces once more. To Prince Andrei's bewilderment, they both began to cry, then kissed again. Mademoiselle Bourienne started crying too. Prince Andrei was clearly uncomfortable, but to the two women it all felt perfectly natural—it apparently never crossed their minds that their meeting could have gone any other way.

"Oh, my dear!... Oh, Mary!..." they exclaimed simultaneously, then laughed. "I dreamed about you last night..." "You weren't expecting us?..." "Oh, Mary, you've gotten thinner!..." "And you've gotten heavier!..."
"I recognized the princess right away," Mademoiselle Bourienne put in.
"And I had no idea!..." Princess Mary exclaimed. "Oh, Andrei—I didn't even see you."

Prince Andrei and his sister took each other's hands and kissed, and he told her she was still the same crybaby she had always been. Princess Mary turned toward her brother, and through her tears the warm, loving, gentle light of her large, luminous eyes—extraordinarily beautiful in that moment—rested on Prince Andrei's face.

The little princess chattered nonstop. Her short, downy upper lip kept dipping to meet her rosy lower lip, then lifting again as her face broke into a smile of gleaming teeth and sparkling eyes. She told them about an accident they'd had on Spassky Hill that could have been serious in her condition, then immediately reported that she'd left all her clothes in Petersburg and heaven knew what she would wear here, and that Andrei had completely changed, and that Kitty Odyntsova had married an old man, and that there was a real suitor for Mary—but they'd discuss that later. Princess Mary watched her brother in silence, her beautiful eyes full of love and sadness. She was clearly following her own train of thought, independent of her sister-in-law's stream of words. In the middle of a description of the latest Petersburg party, she turned to her brother:
"So you're really going to the war, Andrei?" she asked with a sigh.
Lise sighed too.
"Yes—tomorrow, in fact," her brother replied.
"He's leaving me here, God knows why, when he could have had a promotion..."
Princess Mary didn't hear the rest. Following her own thoughts, she turned to her sister-in-law with a tender glance at her figure.
"Is it definite?" she asked.
The little princess's face changed. She sighed and said: "Yes, quite definite. Oh, it's so frightening..."
Her lip dropped. She brought her face close to her sister-in-law's and suddenly began to cry again.
"She needs to rest," Prince Andrei said with a frown. "Don't you, Lise? Take her to your room, and I'll go see Father. How is he? The same as ever?"
"Yes, exactly the same. Though I don't know what you'll make of it," the princess answered cheerfully.

"Same hours? Same walks along the avenues? And the lathe?" Prince Andrei asked with a barely perceptible smile, showing that despite all his love and respect for his father, he was well aware of his quirks.
"The same hours, and the lathe, and the mathematics, and my geometry lessons," Princess Mary said happily, as though geometry were among the greatest pleasures of her life.

When the twenty minutes were up and it was time for the old prince to rise, Tikhon came to summon the young prince. In honor of his son's arrival, the old man made an exception to his routine: he gave orders for Prince Andrei to be admitted to his rooms while he dressed for dinner. The old prince always dressed in the old-fashioned way—an antique-style coat and powdered hair. When Prince Andrei entered his father's dressing room—not wearing the contemptuous expression he put on in drawing rooms, but the lively face he showed when talking with Pierre—the old man was sitting in a large leather armchair, wrapped in a powdering cape, offering his head to Tikhon's ministrations.
"Ah, the warrior! Come to conquer Bonaparte?" the old man said, shaking his powdered head as much as the braid Tikhon was plaiting would allow.
"You'd better deal with him properly, or he'll have us all as his subjects before long! How are you?" And he offered his cheek.

The old man was in high spirits after his pre-dinner nap. (He used to say that a nap after dinner was silver, but before dinner was gold.) He cast fond, sidelong glances at his son from beneath those thick, bushy brows. Prince Andrei went over and kissed his father on the indicated spot. He made no comment on his father's favorite hobby—ridiculing modern-day military leaders, and Bonaparte in particular.
"Yes, Father, I've come with my wife, who is expecting," Prince Andrei said, watching his father's face with eager, respectful attention. "How is your health?"
"Only fools and wastrels get sick, my boy. You know me: I'm busy from morning to night, I'm moderate in everything—naturally I'm well."
"Thank God," said his son, smiling.

"God has nothing to do with it! Now then," he continued, returning to his favorite topic, "tell me how the Germans have been teaching you to fight Bonaparte with this new science of theirs—'strategy,' they call it."
Prince Andrei smiled.
"Give me a chance to catch my breath, Father," he said with a grin that showed his father's eccentricities didn't diminish his love or respect. "I haven't even had time to settle in!"

"Nonsense, nonsense!" the old man cried, tugging at his pigtail to test the braid, and grabbing his son's hand. "The house for your wife is ready. Princess Mary will take her over and show her around—they'll chatter to their hearts' content. That's how women are! I'm glad to have her. Sit down and talk. I understand about Mikhelson's army—and Tolstoy's too... a coordinated offensive... But what's the southern army supposed to do? Prussia is neutral—I know that. And Austria?" he said, rising from his chair and pacing the room while Tikhon trotted behind him, handing over various articles of clothing. "What about Sweden? How will they cross Pomerania?"

Prince Andrei, seeing his father wouldn't let it go, began reluctantly—but gradually with more and more animation, switching unconsciously from Russian to French as was his habit—to explain the campaign plan. He described how an army of ninety thousand was to threaten Prussia to force her out of neutrality and into the war; how part of that force would link up with Swedish troops at Stralsund; how two hundred and twenty thousand Austrians and a hundred thousand Russians would operate in Italy and on the Rhine; how fifty thousand Russians and an equal number of British would land at Naples; and how a combined force of five hundred thousand men was to attack the French from multiple directions. The old prince showed not the slightest interest during this explanation, continuing to dress and walk about as if he weren't listening. Three times he interrupted unexpectedly. Once he stopped the narrative by shouting: "The white one, the white one!"
This meant Tikhon was handing him the wrong waistcoat. Another time he broke in to say:
"And when is she due?" Then, shaking his head disapprovingly: "That's bad! Go on, go on."
The third interruption came as Prince Andrei was wrapping up. The old man began singing in the cracked voice of old age: [Speaking in French] "Marlborough is off to war. God knows when he'll return."
* "Marlborough is going to the wars; God knows when he'll return."
His son only smiled.
"I'm not saying I approve of the plan," the son said. "I'm just telling you what it is. Napoleon has surely drawn up his own plan by now—and it's probably no worse than this one."
"Well, you haven't told me anything new," the old man said, and repeated meditatively, with quick rhythm:
"[Speaking in French] God knows when he'll return. Now go to the dining room."

title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: In October 1805, a Russian army was occupying the villages and towns of the Archduchy of Austria, while fresh regiments still arriving from Russia were settling around the fortress of Braunau and burdening the local residents on whom they were billeted. Braunau served as the headquarters of the commander in chief, Kutuzov.

On October 11, 1805, one of the infantry regiments that had just reached Braunau was halted half a mile from town, waiting to be inspected by the commander in chief. Despite the distinctly un-Russian landscape — fruit orchards, stone fences, tiled roofs, and hills in the distance — and despite the fact that the curious locals staring at the soldiers were not Russian, the regiment looked exactly like any Russian regiment preparing for inspection anywhere in the heart of Russia.

The evening before, an order had come down that the commander in chief would inspect the regiment while on the march. Although the wording was unclear to the regimental commander — there was some question about whether the troops should be in marching order or not — a conference of battalion commanders decided to present the regiment in full parade formation, on the principle that it's always better to bow too low than not low enough. So after a twenty-mile march, the soldiers were kept up all night mending and polishing without a moment's sleep, while adjutants and company commanders calculated and recounted, and by morning the regiment — instead of the straggling, disorderly mob it had been on its march the day before — presented a well-ordered display of two thousand men, each of whom knew his place and his duty, with every button and every strap in position, shining with cleanliness. And not only was the exterior in order; had the commander in chief cared to look beneath the uniforms, he would have found a clean shirt on every man and in every knapsack the regulation number of articles — "needle, soap, and all," as the soldiers liked to say. There was only one problem no one could solve: the state of the men's boots. More than half were full of holes. But this wasn't the regimental commander's fault — he had submitted repeated requests, and the Austrian commissariat had simply never delivered the boots. The regiment had marched some seven hundred miles.

The regimental commander was an elderly, hot-tempered, heavyset general with grizzled eyebrows and whiskers, broader from chest to back than across the shoulders. He wore a brand-new uniform still showing its fold creases and thick gold epaulettes that seemed to stand up rather than lie flat on his massive shoulders. He had the air of a man happily performing one of the most solemn duties of his life. He walked back and forth in front of the ranks, pulling himself up and slightly arching his back at every step. It was clear the commander adored his regiment, took immense pride in it, and thought of nothing else — yet his strutting walk also suggested that military matters were not the only thing on his mind, and that social life and the fair sex occupied no small corner of his thoughts.

"Well, Mikhail Mitrich, sir?" he said, addressing one of the battalion commanders, who pressed forward with a smile. It was obvious they were both in high spirits. "We had our hands full last night. Still, I'd say the regiment doesn't look half bad, eh?"
The battalion commander caught the good-humored irony and laughed.
"It wouldn't be turned off the field even on the Tsaritsin parade ground."
"What's that?" asked the commander.
At that moment, two horsemen appeared on the road from town, where lookouts had been posted. They were an aide-de-camp and a Cossack riding behind him.

The aide-de-camp had been sent to clarify the previous day's ambiguously worded order: the commander in chief wanted to see the regiment exactly as it had been on the march — in greatcoats and packs, without any preparation whatsoever.

An official from the Hofkriegsrath in Vienna had visited Kutuzov the previous day with proposals and demands that he join forces with the army of Archduke Ferdinand and Mack. Kutuzov, who considered this merger inadvisable, intended — among other arguments in support of his position — to show the Austrian general the wretched condition in which the troops arrived from Russia. For this purpose he wanted to meet the regiment in its actual state; the worse it looked, the happier the commander in chief would be. Though the aide-de-camp didn't know these background details, he delivered the definite order: the men were to be in greatcoats and marching order, and the commander in chief would be displeased otherwise. Hearing this, the regimental commander hung his head, shrugged silently, and threw out his arms in frustration.
"A fine mess we've made of it!" he said.

"Didn't I tell you, Mikhail Mitrich? When they said 'on the march,' it meant in greatcoats!" he said reproachfully to the battalion commander. "Oh, my God!" He stepped forward decisively. "Company commanders!" he bellowed in a voice built for commanding. "Sergeants major!... How soon will he be here?" he asked the aide-de-camp with a respectful politeness clearly directed at the personage in question.
"An hour, I'd say."
"Will we have time to change?"
"I couldn't say, General."

The regimental commander walked up to the line himself and ordered the soldiers to change into their greatcoats. Company commanders ran to their companies, sergeants major began scrambling — the greatcoats weren't in the best shape — and instantly the silent, orderly squares began to sway, stretch, and buzz with voices. Soldiers ran in every direction, tossing their knapsacks up with a jerk of the shoulders, pulling straps over their heads, unbuckling overcoats and jamming their arms through the sleeves.

Within half an hour, everything was back in order — only the squares had turned from black to gray. The regimental commander walked with his jerky steps to the front and surveyed the whole formation from a distance.
"What in the — what is this? This!" he shouted, stopping short. "Commander of the third company!"

"Commander of the third company — the general wants you!... Commander to the general... third company to the commander!" The words passed down the lines, and an adjutant ran off to find the missing officer.

When the eager but garbled message finally reached its destination as "The general to the third company!" the missing officer appeared from behind his men and — though he was a middle-aged man not accustomed to running — came trotting awkwardly toward the general, stumbling on his toes. The captain's face wore the anxious look of a schoolboy called on to recite a lesson he hasn't learned. Spots bloomed on his nose, whose redness was clearly the result of heavy drinking, and his mouth twitched nervously. The general looked him up and down as he arrived, panting and slowing his pace.

"You'll be dressing your men in petticoats next! What is this?" the regimental commander barked, jutting his jaw toward a soldier in the third company's ranks who wore a greatcoat of bluish cloth that stood out from all the others. "What have you been doing? The commander in chief is about to arrive and you abandon your post? I'll teach you to put fancy coats on your men for inspection!"
The company commander pressed two fingers ever harder to his cap visor, as if all his salvation lay in that gesture.
"Well? Why don't you answer? Who's that you've got dressed up like a Hungarian?" the commander demanded with grim sarcasm.
"Your excellency..."
"Well? 'Your excellency' what? 'Your excellency'! Nobody seems to know anything around here."
"Your excellency, it's the officer Dolokhov, who was reduced to the ranks," the captain said quietly.
"So? Has he been demoted to field marshal, or to private? If he's a private, he wears regulation uniform like everyone else."
"Your excellency, you gave him permission yourself, on the march."

"Permission? Permission? That's just like you young officers," the regimental commander said, cooling off slightly. "Permission, indeed... You say one word to any of you and then... What?" he added, his irritation flaring again. "I'm asking you to dress your men properly."

He turned to the adjutant and continued down the line with his jerky stride. He was clearly enjoying his own display of anger and looking for another target. Having snapped at one officer over an unpolished badge and at another for a crooked line, he reached the third company.
"How are you standing? Where's your leg? Your leg!" the commander bellowed in a pained voice, though he was still five men away from Dolokhov in his bluish-gray coat.
Dolokhov slowly straightened his bent knee, staring directly at the general's face with clear, insolent eyes.
"Why a blue coat? Take it off... Sergeant major! Change his coat — the ras—" He didn't finish.
"General, I must follow orders, but I am not required to endure —" Dolokhov cut in sharply.
"No talking in the ranks! No talking!"
"— insults," Dolokhov finished, his voice loud, clear, and ringing.
The general's eyes met the soldier's. The general fell silent, tugging angrily at his tight collar.
"I would ask you to kindly change your coat," he said as he turned and walked away.

title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Remounting his horse, Prince Andrew lingered by the battery, watching the puff of smoke from the gun that had fired the shot. His eyes swept rapidly across the broad field, and he could see that the previously motionless French masses had begun to stir, and that there really was a battery on their left. The smoke from it hadn't yet cleared before another puff appeared, followed by the boom of a cannon. The battle had begun. Prince Andrew wheeled his horse around and galloped back to Grunth to find Prince Bagration. Behind him, the cannonade was growing louder and more frequent. Clearly, the Russian guns had started firing back. From the low ground where the parley had taken place that morning came the crackle of musket fire.

Lemarrois had just arrived at a gallop bearing Bonaparte's harsh letter, and Murat, humiliated and desperate to make up for his blunder, had immediately sent his forces forward to attack the center and outflank both Russian wings, hoping to crush this pitiful detachment before evening, before the Emperor himself could arrive.
"It's started. Here it is!" thought Prince Andrew, feeling the blood rush to his heart. "But where—and how—will I find my Toulon?"

Riding past the companies that had been eating porridge and drinking vodka just fifteen minutes ago, he saw the same scene everywhere: soldiers rapidly forming ranks, readying their muskets, and on every face the same fierce eagerness that burned in his own heart. "It's started! Here it is—terrifying but thrilling!" That was what each soldier's and each officer's face seemed to say.

Before he reached the earthworks being thrown up, he saw, in the dull light of the autumn evening, mounted men riding toward him. The one in front, wearing a Cossack cloak and a lambskin cap on a white horse, was Prince Bagration. Prince Andrew pulled up and waited; Bagration reined in his horse, recognized Prince Andrew, and gave him a nod. He kept looking straight ahead while Prince Andrew reported what he had observed.

The feeling—"It's started! Here it is!"—was visible even on Prince Bagration's hard, dark face with its half-shut, sleepy eyes. Prince Andrew studied that impassive face with anxious curiosity, wanting to know what, if anything, this man was thinking and feeling at that moment. "Is there actually anything behind that expressionless mask?" Prince Andrew wondered. Bagration inclined his head to signal agreement with what Prince Andrew told him and said, "Very good," in a tone suggesting that everything happening was exactly what he'd expected. Prince Andrew, out of breath from his hard ride, spoke quickly. Bagration, pronouncing his words with an Eastern accent, spoke especially slowly, as though to demonstrate that there was no need for haste. Still, he set his horse to a trot toward Tushin's battery. Prince Andrew followed with the rest of the staff. Behind Bagration rode a staff officer, the prince's personal adjutant, Zherkov, an orderly officer, the duty staff officer on a handsome bob-tailed horse, and a civilian—an accountant who had asked permission to observe the battle out of curiosity. The accountant, a stout man with a round face, looked around with a naive smile of delight and cut a strange figure among the hussars, Cossacks, and adjutants, bouncing along in his wool coat on a horse fitted with a convoy officer's saddle.
"He wants to see a battle," Zherkov said to Bolkonsky, nodding toward the accountant. "But he's already got a stomachache."
"Oh, stop it!" said the accountant with a beaming but slightly sly smile, flattered to be the butt of Zherkov's joke and deliberately playing up his own foolishness.
"It is very strange, mon Monsieur Prince," said the staff officer. (He remembered there was some special way to address a prince in French, but couldn't quite get it right.)
By now they were all approaching Tushin's battery, and a cannonball struck the ground in front of them.
"What was that that fell?" asked the accountant with a guileless smile.
"A French pancake," Zherkov replied.
"So that's what they fire at you? How frightening!" said the accountant.

He seemed to swell with satisfaction. He'd barely finished speaking when they heard another unexpectedly violent whistling that suddenly ended with a thud into something soft—f-f-flop!—and a Cossack riding slightly to the right and behind the accountant crashed to the earth along with his horse. Zherkov and the staff officer ducked over their saddles and yanked their horses aside. The accountant stopped, staring at the fallen Cossack with wide-eyed curiosity. The Cossack was dead, but the horse still thrashed.

Prince Bagration squinted, glanced around, and, seeing what had caused the commotion, turned away with indifference, as if to say, "Is this really worth stopping for?" He reined in his horse with the skill of an expert rider and, bending slightly, freed his saber, which had caught in his cloak. It was an old-fashioned saber, not the kind in common use anymore. Prince Andrew remembered the story of how Suvorov had given his saber to Bagration in Italy, and the memory felt especially right at that moment. They had reached the battery where Prince Andrew had stood earlier surveying the field.
"Whose company?" Prince Bagration asked an artilleryman standing by an ammunition wagon.
He asked, "Whose company?" but what he really meant was, "You're not scared up here, are you?" And the artilleryman understood perfectly.
"Captain Tushin's, your excellency!" shouted a red-haired, freckled gunner in a cheerful voice, standing at attention.
"Right, right," Bagration muttered, as if turning something over in his mind, and rode past the limbers to the farthest cannon.

As he approached, a deafening blast erupted from it, and in the sudden cloud of smoke that enveloped the gun, they could see the crew straining to roll it quickly back into position. A huge, broad-shouldered gunner—Number One—stood with legs wide apart, gripping a sponge-staff, and sprang to the wheel. Number Two, his hands trembling, rammed a charge into the cannon's mouth. Captain Tushin, short and round-shouldered, stumbled over the tail of the gun carriage as he came forward and, not noticing the general, shaded his eyes with his small hand and peered out at the enemy.
"Elevate two lines more and it'll be perfect," he called out in his thin voice, trying to sound bold—a tone that didn't suit his slight frame at all. "Number Two! Fire, Medvedev!"

Bagration called to him, and Tushin, raising three fingers to his cap in a bashful, awkward gesture—less like a military salute than a priest's blessing—approached the general. Although Tushin's guns were supposed to be covering the valley, he had been lobbing incendiary shells at the village of Schon Grabern, which lay directly ahead, where large masses of French troops were advancing.

No one had given Tushin specific orders about where to aim, but after consulting his sergeant major Zakharchenko, whom he deeply respected, he'd decided on his own that setting the village on fire would be useful. "Very good!" said Bagration in response to the officer's report, and began carefully surveying the entire battlefield spread before him. The French had pushed closest on the right. Below the heights where the Kiev regiment was stationed, in the hollow where the stream flowed, came the stirring, rolling crackle of musket fire. And much further to the right, beyond the dragoons, a staff officer pointed out to Bagration a French column that was moving to outflank them. To the left, the horizon was bounded by the nearby woods. Prince Bagration ordered two battalions from the center sent to reinforce the right flank. The staff officer dared to point out that if those battalions left, the guns would be completely unprotected. Bagration turned to the officer and stared at him in silence with his dull eyes. Prince Andrew felt the officer's concern was perfectly justified, and that there really was no good answer to it. But at that moment an adjutant came galloping up with a message from the colonel commanding the troops in the hollow: massive French forces were bearing down on them, and his regiment was falling apart, retreating toward the Kiev grenadiers. Prince Bagration gave a nod of acknowledgment. He rode off to the right at a walk and sent an adjutant to the dragoons with orders to attack the French. But this adjutant returned half an hour later with the news that the dragoon commander had already pulled back behind the ravine—heavy fire had been concentrated on his position and he was losing men for nothing—so he'd pushed some sharpshooters into the woods instead.
"Very good!" said Bagration.

As he rode away from the battery, firing broke out on the left too. Since it was too far for him to reach the left flank in time, Bagration sent Zherkov to tell the general in command there—the same one who had paraded his regiment before Kutuzov at Braunau—to pull back as fast as possible behind the hollow to the rear, since the right flank probably couldn't hold the enemy's assault much longer. As for Tushin and the battalion supporting his battery, they were completely forgotten. Prince Andrew listened closely to Bagration's exchanges with the various officers and the orders he issued, and to his surprise realized that no real orders were being given at all. What Bagration actually did was try to make it appear that everything happening—whether by necessity, by chance, or by the initiative of subordinate commanders—was being done, if not by his direct command, then at least in keeping with his intentions. Prince Andrew noticed, though, that despite the fact that events unfolded independently of Bagration's will, the man's tact made his presence genuinely valuable. Officers who approached him with worried faces became calm; soldiers and officers greeted him warmly, visibly perked up around him, and clearly wanted to show their bravery in front of him.

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Old Prince Bolkonsky received a letter from Prince Vasili in November 1805, announcing that he and his son would be visiting. 'I'm going on an inspection tour, and of course I won't mind an extra seventy miles to see you, my esteemed benefactor,' wrote Prince Vasili. 'My son Anatole is traveling with me on his way to the army, so I hope you'll allow him to personally express the deep respect that, following his father's example, he feels for you.'
"It seems we won't need to introduce Mary to society—suitors are coming to us on their own," the little princess carelessly remarked upon hearing the news.
Prince Bolkonsky frowned but said nothing.
Two weeks after the letter, Prince Vasili's servants arrived one evening ahead of him, and he and his son came the next day.

Old Bolkonsky had always had a low opinion of Prince Vasili's character, and even more so recently, since under Paul and Alexander, Prince Vasili had risen to high positions and honors. Now, from the hints in his letter and from the little princess's comments, he saw where this was heading, and his low opinion turned to contemptuous hostility. He snorted whenever Prince Vasili's name came up. On the day of the visit, the old prince was especially irritable and out of sorts. Whether he was in a bad mood because Prince Vasili was coming, or whether his bad mood made the visit especially annoying, he was difficult. That morning, Tikhon had already warned the architect not to go to the prince with his report.
"Hear how he's walking?" said Tikhon, drawing the architect's attention to the sound of the prince's footsteps. "Flat on his heels—we know what that means..."

Still, at nine o'clock, the prince put on his velvet coat with a sable collar and cap and went out for his usual walk. It had snowed the day before, and the path to the greenhouse that the prince always took had been swept clean. The marks of the broom were still visible in the snow, and a shovel had been left stuck in one of the snowbanks lining both sides of the path. The prince walked through the conservatories, the servants' quarters, and the outbuildings, frowning and silent.
"Can a sleigh get through?" he asked his steward, a dignified man who resembled his master in manner and appearance, as they walked back toward the house.
"The snow is deep. I'm having the drive swept, your honor."
The prince nodded and went up to the porch. 'Thank God,' thought the steward, 'the storm has passed!'
"It would have been hard to drive up, your honor," the steward added. "I heard that a minister is coming to visit, your honor."
The prince spun around and fixed his eyes on the steward, frowning.

"What? A minister? What minister? Who gave those orders?" he snapped in his shrill, harsh voice. "The road isn't swept for my daughter the princess, but for a minister! For me, there are no ministers!"
"Your honor, I thought—"

"You thought!" the prince shouted, his words coming faster and more garbled. "You thought!... Scoundrels! Idiots!... I'll teach you to think!" And he raised his walking stick and would have struck Alpatych, the steward, if the man hadn't instinctively jumped back. "Thought... Idiots..." the prince shouted.

But although Alpatych, frightened by his own boldness in dodging the blow, stepped forward with his bald head bowed submissively—or perhaps for that very reason—the prince, though he kept shouting "Idiots! Throw the snow back on the road!" didn't raise his stick again and hurried into the house.

Before dinner, Princess Mary and Mademoiselle Bourienne, who knew the prince was in a bad mood, stood waiting for him. Mademoiselle Bourienne had a bright expression that said, 'I know nothing, I'm the same as always,' while Princess Mary was pale, frightened, with downcast eyes. What she found hardest to bear was knowing that at times like these she should act like Mademoiselle Bourienne, but couldn't. She thought: 'If I act as if nothing's wrong, he'll think I don't care. But if I look sad and gloomy, he'll say—as he has before—that I'm sulking.'
The prince looked at his daughter's frightened face and snorted.
"Fool... or dunce!" he muttered.
"And the other one isn't here either. They've been gossiping," he thought, referring to the little princess, who wasn't in the dining room.
"Where is the princess?" he asked. "Hiding?"
"She isn't feeling well," Mademoiselle Bourienne answered with a bright smile. "She won't be coming down. It's natural in her condition."
"Hm! Hm!" the prince muttered, sitting down.

His plate seemed not quite clean to him. Pointing at a spot, he flung it away. Tikhon caught it and passed it to a footman. The little princess wasn't actually ill, but she was so terrified of the prince that, hearing he was in a bad temper, she had decided not to come down.
"I'm worried about the baby," she told Mademoiselle Bourienne. "Who knows what a fright could do."

In general, life at Bald Hills meant constant fear for the little princess, mixed with a feeling of dislike for the old prince that she didn't acknowledge because the fear was so much stronger. The prince returned that dislike, but it was overwhelmed by his contempt for her. Once the little princess had settled in at Bald Hills, she took a particular liking to Mademoiselle Bourienne, spent whole days with her, asked her to sleep in her room, and often talked with her about the old prince, criticizing him.

"So we're going to have visitors, Prince?" said Mademoiselle Bourienne, unfolding her white napkin with her pink fingers. "His Excellency Prince Vasili Kuragin and his son, I understand?" she said, as if asking for confirmation.

"Hm—his excellency is a lightweight... I got him his position," the prince said dismissively. "Why his son is coming, I have no idea. Maybe Princess Elizabeth and Princess Mary know. I don't want him." He looked at his blushing daughter. "Are you unwell today? Eh? Scared of the 'minister,' as that fool Alpatych called him this morning?"
"No, Father."

Although Mademoiselle Bourienne had chosen her topic poorly, she didn't stop talking. She chattered about the conservatories and a flower that had just bloomed. After the soup, the prince became more pleasant.
After dinner he went to visit his daughter-in-law. The little princess was sitting at a small table chatting with Masha, her maid. She turned pale when she saw her father-in-law.
She had changed a great deal. She was now plain rather than pretty. Her cheeks had hollowed, her lip curled up, and her eyes were drawn down.
"Yes, I feel some pressure," she said in answer to the prince's question about how she was feeling.
"Do you need anything?"
"No, thank you, Father."
"Very well then."
He left the room and went to the vestibule, where Alpatych stood with his head bowed.
"Was the snow put back?"
"Yes, your excellency. Forgive me, for heaven's sake... It was just my stupidity."
"Fine, fine," the prince interrupted, and with his strange, forced laugh, he held out his hand for Alpatych to kiss, then went to his study.

Prince Vasili arrived that evening. He was met on the drive by coachmen and servants who, shouting loudly, dragged his sleighs up to one of the lodges over the road that had been deliberately piled with snow.
Prince Vasili and Anatole were given separate rooms.

Anatole, having taken off his coat, sat with arms crossed before a table, smilingly and absent-mindedly fixing his large, handsome eyes on one corner. He viewed his entire life as one continuous round of entertainment that someone, for some reason, had to provide for him. He regarded this visit to a grumpy old man and a rich, ugly heiress the same way. It might all turn out quite nicely and amusingly. 'And why not marry her if she really has that much money? That never hurts,' thought Anatole.

He shaved and perfumed himself with the care and elegance that had become second nature, and with his handsome head held high, entered his father's room with his naturally cheerful and confident air. Prince Vasili's two valets were busy dressing him. He looked around with great animation and gave his son a friendly nod as he entered, as if to say: 'Yes, that's exactly how I want you to look.'
"Seriously though, Father, is she really that ugly?" Anatole asked, as if picking up a conversation they'd had many times on the journey.
"Enough! Don't be ridiculous! Above all, try to be respectful and careful with the old prince."
"If he starts making trouble, I'm leaving," said Anatole. "I can't stand those old men! Right?"
"Remember, everything depends on this for you."

Meanwhile, it wasn't just the servants who knew the minister and his son had arrived—both their appearances had been described in minute detail. Princess Mary sat alone in her room, trying in vain to calm her anxiety.

"Why did they write? Why did Lise tell me about it? It can never happen!" she said, looking at herself in the mirror. "How will I walk into the drawing room? Even if I like him, I can't be myself with him now." The mere thought of her father's look filled her with dread. The little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne had already received from Masha, the lady's maid, a thorough report on how handsome the minister's son was, with his rosy cheeks and dark eyebrows, and how his father had barely managed to drag his legs upstairs while the son had bounded up like an eagle, three steps at a time. With this intelligence in hand, the little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne, whose chattering voices had been audible from the hallway, went into Princess Mary's room.
"Did you know they've arrived, Marie?" said the little princess, waddling in and sinking heavily into an armchair.

She had changed out of her usual loose morning gown and put on one of her best dresses. Her hair was done up and her face was lively—though this couldn't hide how much thinner and paler she had become. Dressed as she used to be in Petersburg society, it was even more obvious how much plainer she looked now. Some subtle touch had been added to Mademoiselle Bourienne's outfit that made her fresh, pretty face even more appealing.

"What—are you going to stay like that, dear princess?" she began. "They're going to announce the gentlemen in the drawing room any minute and we'll have to go down, and you haven't done anything with yourself!"

The little princess jumped up, rang for the maid, and with cheerful energy began planning how to dress Princess Mary. Princess Mary's pride was wounded by the fact that a suitor's arrival excited her, and even more by her companions' complete inability to imagine she might feel differently about it. To tell them she was embarrassed—for herself and for them—would be to reveal her agitation. To refuse their help would only prolong their teasing and insistence. She blushed, her beautiful eyes dimmed, red blotches appeared on her face, and it took on the unattractive, long-suffering expression it so often wore as she submitted to Mademoiselle Bourienne and Lise. Both women sincerely tried to make her pretty. She was so plain that neither could see her as a rival, so they set about dressing her with genuine conviction—the unshakable female belief that clothes can make any face pretty.

"No, really, dear, this dress won't do," said Lise, studying Princess Mary from a distance. "You have a maroon dress—go get it. Seriously! Your whole life might depend on this. But this one is too light, it's not right for you!"

It wasn't the dress but Princess Mary's face and whole figure that weren't attractive. But neither Mademoiselle Bourienne nor the little princess could see this. They still believed that if a blue ribbon were placed in her hair, the hair pinned up, and the blue scarf lowered on the best maroon dress, everything would be fine. They forgot that the anxious face and the figure couldn't be changed, and that no matter how much they altered the setting and accessories around that face, it would still look sad and plain. After two or three outfit changes—to which Princess Mary meekly submitted—once her hair had been piled on top of her head (a style that completely altered and worsened her appearance) and she had put on a maroon dress with a pale-blue scarf, the little princess circled her twice, adjusting a fold here, straightening the scarf there, tilting her head this way and that.

"No, it won't work," she said firmly, clasping her hands. "No, Marie, this dress really doesn't suit you. I prefer you in your little gray everyday dress. Please, do it for my sake. Katie," she called to the maid, "bring the princess her gray dress, and you'll see, Mademoiselle Bourienne, how I'll fix it up." She smiled with the anticipated pleasure of an artist.

But when Katie brought the gray dress, Princess Mary sat motionless before the mirror, staring at her face. In the reflection she could see her eyes filling with tears and her mouth quivering, about to burst into sobs.
"Come, dear princess," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, "just one more little effort."
The little princess took the dress from the maid and came over to Princess Mary.
"Now we'll make something simple and flattering," she said.
The three voices—hers, Mademoiselle Bourienne's, and Katie's, who was laughing at something—blended together in a cheerful sound, like birdsong.
"No, leave me alone," said Princess Mary.

Her voice sounded so serious and so sad that the birdsong stopped at once. They looked at her beautiful, large, thoughtful eyes, shining with tears and unspoken thoughts, gazing imploringly at them—and understood that insisting would be useless, even cruel.

"At least change your hairstyle," said the little princess. "Didn't I tell you," she added, turning reproachfully to Mademoiselle Bourienne, "that Mary's face doesn't suit that style at all? Not at all! Please change it."
"Leave me alone, please leave me alone! It's all the same to me," answered a voice struggling with tears.

Mademoiselle Bourienne and the little princess had to admit to themselves that Princess Mary looked very plain like this—worse than usual—but it was too late. She gazed at them with an expression they both knew well: thoughtful and sad. This look never frightened anyone (she was never intimidating), but they knew that when it appeared, she became silent and nothing could change her mind.
"You will change it, won't you?" said Lise. When Princess Mary didn't answer, she left the room.

Princess Mary was left alone. She didn't do as Lise asked; she not only kept her hair as it was but didn't even glance in the mirror. Letting her arms fall helplessly, she sat with downcast eyes and lost herself in thought. In her imagination, a husband appeared—a man, strong, commanding, and strangely attractive—and carried her away into a completely different, happy world. She imagined a child, her own—like the one she had seen yesterday in her nurse's daughter's arms—at her breast, with the husband standing beside her, gazing tenderly at her and the baby. 'But no, it's impossible—I'm too ugly,' she thought.
"Please come to tea. The prince will be out in a moment," came the maid's voice from the door.

She stirred and was appalled at what she had been thinking. Before going downstairs, she went into the room where the icons hung and stood before the dark face of a large icon of the Savior, lit by a lamp, her hands folded in prayer. A painful doubt filled her soul. Could the joy of love—earthly love for a man—really be meant for her? In her dreams of marriage, Princess Mary imagined happiness and children, but her deepest, most hidden longing was for earthly love. The harder she tried to conceal this feeling from others and from herself, the stronger it grew. 'Oh God,' she said, 'how can I overcome these temptations? How can I give up these sinful dreams and peacefully fulfill Your will?' And as soon as she asked the question, God answered in her own heart. 'Desire nothing for yourself. Seek nothing. Be not anxious or envious. The future—both mankind's and your own—must remain hidden from you. But live so that you are ready for anything. If God wills that you be tested in marriage, be ready to fulfill His will.' With this comforting thought—though still harboring hope for the fulfillment of her forbidden earthly longing—Princess Mary sighed, crossed herself, and went downstairs, thinking not of her dress or hairstyle or how she would enter or what she would say. What did any of that matter compared to the will of God, without whose care not a single hair falls from anyone's head?

title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: When Princess Mary came downstairs, Prince Vasili and his son were already in the drawing room, talking with the little princess and Mademoiselle Bourienne. As she entered with her heavy step, walking on her heels, the gentlemen and Mademoiselle Bourienne stood up, and the little princess pointed her out to the guests: 'Here's Marie!' Princess Mary saw them all and registered every detail. She saw Prince Vasili's face go serious for an instant when he noticed her, then immediately break into a smile again. She saw the little princess watching curiously for the impression 'Marie' would make. She saw Mademoiselle Bourienne with her ribbon and pretty face, looking unusually animated, her eyes fixed on him. But him she couldn't really see—she only saw something large, brilliant, and handsome moving toward her. Prince Vasili approached first, and she kissed the bold forehead that bent over her hand, answering his question by saying that she remembered him perfectly well. Then Anatole came up. She still couldn't see him clearly. She only felt a soft hand take hers firmly, and her lips touched a white forehead framed by beautiful light-brown hair that smelled of pomade. When she finally looked up, she was struck by his beauty. Anatole stood with his right thumb hooked under a button of his uniform, his chest out, his back straight, gently shifting his weight on one foot, his head tilted slightly, looking at the princess with a beaming face—not speaking and obviously not thinking about her at all. Anatole wasn't quick-witted or eloquent in conversation, but he had the invaluable social gift of composure and unshakable self-assurance. If a man who lacks confidence stays silent at a first meeting, betraying awareness of the awkwardness and anxiety to fill it, the effect is bad. But Anatole was silent, he shifted his weight, and he smiled while studying the princess's hair arrangement. He clearly could have stayed silent like this for a very long time. 'If anyone finds this silence uncomfortable, they can talk, but I don't feel like it,' he seemed to say. Beyond this, in his manner with women, Anatole had a way that particularly inspired curiosity, awe, and even love—a casual awareness of his own superiority. It was as though he were saying to them: 'I know you. I know you very well. But why should I bother with you? You'd be delighted, of course.' Perhaps he didn't actually think this when meeting women—most likely he didn't, since he rarely thought much at all—but his looks and behavior gave that impression. The princess sensed it, and as if wanting to show that she didn't even expect to interest him, she turned to his father. The conversation was lively and animated, thanks to Princess Lise's voice and her little downy lip curving over her white teeth. She greeted Prince Vasili with the playful manner common to chatty, lively people—the kind that assumes a shared history of private jokes and fond memories between speaker and listener, even when no such history exists. Prince Vasili played along easily, and the little princess also drew Anatole, whom she barely knew, into these entertaining recollections of things that had never happened. Mademoiselle Bourienne joined in too, and even Princess Mary felt herself pleasantly pulled into these cheerful, fictional reminiscences.

"Here at least we'll have you all to ourselves, dear prince," the little princess said to Prince Vasili in French. "It's not like at Annette's parties, where you always ran off. You remember dear Annette!"
Anna Pavlovna.
"Oh, but you won't lecture me about politics like Annette!"
"And our little tea table?"
"Oh, yes!"

"Why were you never at Annette's?" the little princess asked Anatole. "Oh, I know, I know," she said with a sly look, "your brother Hippolyte told me all about your adventures. Oh!" And she wagged her finger at him. "I've even heard about your escapades in Paris!"

"And didn't Hippolyte tell you," asked Prince Vasili, turning to his son and grabbing the little princess's arm as if she were about to escape, "how he pined for the dear princess, and how she showed him the door? Oh, she's a pearl among women, princess," he added, turning to Princess Mary.
When Paris was mentioned, Mademoiselle Bourienne seized the chance to join in.

She asked if it had been long since Anatole left Paris and whether he had enjoyed it there. Anatole answered the Frenchwoman readily and, studying her with a smile, chatted with her about her homeland. When he noticed the pretty little Bourienne, Anatole decided that life at Bald Hills might not be boring after all. 'Not bad at all!' he thought, looking her over. 'Not bad at all, that little companion! Hopefully she'll come along when we're married. She's quite charming.'
The little one is charming.

The old prince took his time dressing in his study, frowning and thinking about what to do. These visitors annoyed him. 'What are Prince Vasili and that son of his to me? Prince Vasili is a shallow braggart, and his son is probably a fine specimen,' he grumbled to himself. What really angered him was that the visit forced him to face a question he always tried to suppress, one about which he was always dishonest with himself: could he ever bring himself to give up his daughter and let her marry? The prince never asked himself the question directly, knowing he would have to answer it honestly, and honesty clashed not just with his feelings but with the very possibility of his life. Life without Princess Mary—little as he seemed to value her—was unthinkable to him. 'Why should she marry?' he thought. 'To be miserable, that's certain. Look at Lise, married to Andrew—you'd think a better husband couldn't be found these days—but is she happy? And who would marry Mary for love? She's plain and awkward! They'd only want her for her connections and money. There are plenty of women living unmarried, and they're happier for it.' So thought Prince Bolkonsky while dressing. Yet the question he kept putting off demanded an immediate answer. Prince Vasili had brought his son with the obvious intention of proposing, and today or tomorrow he would likely expect an answer. His birth and social position were acceptable. 'Well, I have nothing against it,' the prince said to himself, 'but he has to be worthy of her. And that's what we'll find out.'
"That's what we'll see! That's what we'll see!" he said aloud.

He entered the drawing room with his usual brisk step, glancing quickly around the room. He noticed the little princess's change of dress, Mademoiselle Bourienne's ribbon, Princess Mary's unflattering hairstyle, Mademoiselle Bourienne's and Anatole's smiles, and his daughter's loneliness amid the general conversation. 'Dressed herself up like a fool!' he thought irritably, looking at her. 'No shame! And he ignores her!'
He went straight up to Prince Vasili.
"Well! Hello! Hello! Good to see you!"
"Friendship laughs at distance," Prince Vasili began in his usual rapid, confident, familiar tone. "Here is my second son. Please be kind to him."
Prince Bolkonsky studied Anatole.
"Fine young man! Fine young man!" he said. "Well, come give me a kiss." And he offered his cheek.
Anatole kissed the old man and studied him with curiosity and perfect composure, waiting for the eccentric behavior his father had warned him about.

Prince Bolkonsky sat down in his usual corner of the sofa and, pulling up an armchair for Prince Vasili, gestured for him to sit. He began asking about politics and the news, seeming to listen carefully to what Prince Vasili said while constantly glancing at Princess Mary.
"So they're writing from Potsdam already?" he said, repeating Prince Vasili's last words. Then he suddenly got up and walked over to his daughter.

"Is that how you dress for visitors, eh?" he said. "Very nice, very nice! You've done your hair in a new way for the guests, and in front of the guests I'm telling you: never again dare change your appearance without my permission."
"It was my fault, Father," the little princess interjected, blushing.
"You may do as you please," Prince Bolkonsky told his daughter-in-law with a bow, "but she doesn't need to make herself look ridiculous—she's plain enough as it is."
And he sat down again, paying no more attention to his daughter, who was in tears.
"On the contrary, that hairstyle suits the princess very well," said Prince Vasili.
"Now then, young prince—what's your name?" said Prince Bolkonsky, turning to Anatole. "Come here, let's talk and get to know each other."
"Now the fun begins," thought Anatole, sitting down beside the old prince with a smile.

"Well, my boy, I hear you were educated abroad—not taught to read by the village deacon, like your father and me. Tell me, are you serving in the Horse Guards?" asked the old man, scrutinizing Anatole closely.
"No, I've been transferred to a line regiment," said Anatole, barely suppressing a laugh.
"Ah! Good thing. So, my boy, you want to serve the Tsar and the country? It's wartime. A fine fellow like you should serve. Well, are you heading to the front?"
"No, Prince, our regiment has moved to the front, but I'm attached... what am I attached to, Papa?" said Anatole, turning to his father with a laugh.
"Splendid soldier, splendid! 'What am I attached to!' Ha, ha, ha!" laughed Prince Bolkonsky, and Anatole laughed even harder. Suddenly the old prince frowned.
"You may go," he told Anatole.
Anatole returned to the ladies with a smile.
"So you had him educated abroad, Prince Vasili?" said the old prince.
"I did my best for him, and I can assure you the education there is much better than ours."

"Yes, everything is different nowadays, everything has changed. The boy's a fine fellow, a fine fellow! Well, come with me." He took Prince Vasili by the arm and led him to his study. As soon as they were alone, Prince Vasili laid out his hopes and intentions.

"What, do you think I'd stop her? That I can't bear to part with her?" the old prince said angrily. "What an idea! I'm ready tomorrow! Only let me tell you, I want to know my future son-in-law better. You know my principles—everything in the open! I'll ask her tomorrow, with you there. If she's willing, then he can stay. He can stay and I'll observe him." He snorted. "Let her marry—it's all the same to me!" he shouted in the same piercing voice he had used when saying goodbye to his son.

"I'll be frank with you," said Prince Vasili, in the tone of a cunning man who has decided there's no point being cunning with someone so sharp. "You know people, you see right through them. Anatole is no genius, but he's an honest, good-hearted young man—an excellent son and kinsman."
"Fine, fine, we'll see!"

As always happens when women live alone for a long time without male company, the arrival of Anatole made all three women of Prince Bolkonsky's household feel that their lives up to that point hadn't been real. Their powers of thinking, feeling, and observing increased tenfold, and their existence, which seemed to have been spent in darkness, was suddenly filled with new, meaningful light.

Princess Mary became completely oblivious to her face and hair. The open, handsome face of the man who might become her husband consumed all her attention. He seemed to her kind, brave, determined, manly, and generous. She felt certain of it. Thousands of dreams about family life rose endlessly in her imagination. She tried to push them away and hide them.

"But am I being too cold with him?" the princess wondered. "I'm trying to hold back because deep down I already feel too close to him. But he can't know what I'm thinking and might believe I don't like him."
And Princess Mary tried—but couldn't manage—to be warm to her new guest. 'Poor girl, she's hopelessly ugly!' thought Anatole.

Mademoiselle Bourienne, also stirred by Anatole's arrival, had quite different thoughts. A beautiful young woman with no real status, no family, not even a country of her own, she certainly hadn't intended to devote her life to serving Prince Bolkonsky, reading aloud to him, and being Princess Mary's companion. Mademoiselle Bourienne had long been waiting for a Russian prince who would recognize at a glance her superiority over the plain, badly dressed, ungainly Russian princesses, fall in love with her, and carry her away. And here at last was a Russian prince. She had a story, heard from her aunt but embellished in her own imagination, that she loved to replay in her mind. It was about a girl who had been seduced, and whose poor mother appeared to reproach her for giving herself to a man without marriage. Mademoiselle Bourienne was often moved to tears as she imagined telling this story to him, her seducer. And now he, a real Russian prince, had appeared. He would carry her off, and then her poor mother would appear, and he would marry her. So her future took shape in Mademoiselle Bourienne's mind even as she chatted with Anatole about Paris. It wasn't calculation guiding her—she didn't even stop to think about what she should do—but all of this had been familiar to her for so long that now, with Anatole present, it simply arranged itself around him, and she wished and tried to please him as much as possible.

The little princess, like a retired warhorse hearing the trumpet, unconsciously and completely forgetting her condition, prepared for the familiar thrill of flirtation—without ulterior motive or inner struggle, with simple, lighthearted pleasure.

Although Anatole usually played the role of a man weary of being chased by women, his vanity was flattered by the sight of his power over these three women. Besides that, he was beginning to feel for the pretty, provocative Mademoiselle Bourienne that passionate, animal desire that tended to seize him suddenly and drive him to the most reckless behavior.

After tea, the group moved to the sitting room and Princess Mary was asked to play the clavichord. Anatole, laughing and in high spirits, leaned on his elbows facing her, next to Mademoiselle Bourienne. Princess Mary felt his gaze with a painful, joyful emotion. Her favorite sonata carried her into a deeply poetic inner world, and the look she felt on her made that world even more beautiful. But Anatole's eyes, though aimed at her, were actually focused on Mademoiselle Bourienne's little foot, which he was nudging with his own under the clavichord. Mademoiselle Bourienne was looking at Princess Mary too, and in her lovely eyes there was an expression of fearful excitement and hope that was new to the princess.

"How she loves me!" thought Princess Mary. "How happy I am now, and how happy I could be with such a friend and such a husband! A husband? Is it really possible?" she thought, not daring to look at his face but still feeling his eyes on her.

That evening, after supper, as everyone was about to retire, Anatole kissed Princess Mary's hand. She didn't know where she found the courage, but she looked straight into his handsome face as it came close to her nearsighted eyes. After Princess Mary, he went up and kissed Mademoiselle Bourienne's hand. (This wasn't proper etiquette, but he did everything with such easy confidence!) Mademoiselle Bourienne blushed and gave the princess a frightened glance.

"What sensitivity!" thought the princess. "Is it possible that Amélie"—Mademoiselle Bourienne—"thinks I could be jealous of her and fail to appreciate her pure devotion to me?" She went over and warmly kissed her. Anatole then went to kiss the little princess's hand.
"No! No! No! When your father writes to tell me you've been behaving yourself, I'll let you kiss my hand. Not before!" she said. And with a teasing smile, wagging her finger, she left the room.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Soon after his admission to the Masonic Brotherhood, Pierre went to the Kiev province, where he had the greatest number of serfs, carrying with him detailed instructions he had written for his own guidance on what to do with his estates.

When he reached Kiev, he summoned all his stewards to the head office and laid out his intentions and wishes. He told them that steps would be taken immediately to free his serfs — and until then, they were not to be overworked, nursing mothers were not to be sent to labor, assistance was to be given to the serfs, punishments were to be educational rather than physical, and hospitals, asylums, and schools were to be established on all the estates. Some of the stewards — among them semi-literate foremen — listened with alarm, supposing these words meant the young count was unhappy with their management and their embezzlement. Some, after their initial fright, were amused by Pierre's lisp and the unfamiliar words. Others simply enjoyed hearing the master talk. But the cleverest among them, including the chief steward, understood from this speech exactly how to manage the master for their own benefit.

The chief steward expressed great sympathy with Pierre's plans, but pointed out that besides these changes it would be necessary to review the overall state of affairs, which was far from satisfactory.

Despite Count Bezukhov's enormous wealth — since he had come into an income reportedly amounting to five hundred thousand rubles a year — Pierre felt himself far poorer than when his father had given him an allowance of ten thousand. He had a rough sense of the following budget:

About 80,000 went in payments on all the estates to the Land Bank; about 30,000 for the upkeep of the Moscow estate, the town house, and allowances to the three princesses; about 15,000 in pensions and the same for asylums; 150,000 in alimony to the countess; about 70,000 for interest on debts. Construction of a new church, previously begun, had cost about 10,000 in each of the last two years, and he didn't know how the rest — about 100,000 rubles — was spent. Almost every year he had to borrow. Besides this, the chief steward wrote annually about fires and bad harvests, or about the need to rebuild factories and workshops. So the first task Pierre faced was one for which he had very little talent or inclination — practical business.

He discussed estate affairs every day with his chief steward, but felt that none of it moved anything forward. He sensed that these consultations were disconnected from real life and didn't make things happen. On one hand, the chief steward painted the worst possible picture, emphasizing the need to pay off debts and undertake new projects with serf labor — to which Pierre wouldn't agree. On the other hand, Pierre demanded that steps be taken to liberate the serfs, which the steward deflected by pointing out that the Land Bank loans must be paid off first, making immediate emancipation impossible.

The steward didn't say outright that it couldn't be done, but suggested selling the forests in Kostroma province, the land along the lower river, and the Crimean estate — all of which involved, according to him, such complicated procedures — injunctions, petitions, permits, and so on — that Pierre became thoroughly bewildered and could only reply:
"Yes, yes, do that."

Pierre lacked the practical persistence needed to manage the business himself, so he disliked it and only pretended to the steward that he was paying attention. The steward, for his part, pretended to the count that these consultations were extremely valuable for the proprietor and troublesome for himself.

In Kiev, Pierre encountered some people he knew, and strangers rushed to make the acquaintance of the rich newcomer, the largest landowner in the province. Temptations targeting Pierre's greatest weakness — the one he had confessed at his Lodge initiation — were so powerful that he couldn't resist them. Once again whole days, weeks, and months passed in a blur of evening parties, dinners, lunches, and balls, leaving him no time for reflection — just like in Petersburg. Instead of the new life he had planned, he was living the same old life, only in different surroundings.

Of the three Masonic precepts, Pierre realized he was failing the one that required every Mason to set an example of moral living, and of the seven virtues he lacked two: morality and the love of death. He consoled himself with the thought that he was fulfilling another precept — reforming humanity — and possessed other virtues: love of his neighbor and especially generosity.

In the spring of 1807 he decided to return to Petersburg. On the way, he planned to visit all his estates and see for himself how his orders had been carried out, and what condition the serfs were in — the serfs God had entrusted to his care and whom he intended to help.

The chief steward, who considered the young count's schemes nearly insane — unprofitable for himself, for the count, and for the serfs — had made some concessions. While continuing to represent the liberation of the serfs as impractical, he arranged for large buildings — schools, hospitals, and asylums — to be erected on all the estates before the master arrived. Everywhere preparations were made, not for ceremonious welcomes (which he knew Pierre wouldn't like), but for touchingly religious ones, with offerings of icons and the bread and salt of hospitality — just the kind that, in his understanding of the master, would impress and deceive him.

The southern spring, the comfortable, rapid travel in a Viennese carriage, and the solitude of the road all had a cheering effect on Pierre. His estates — which he had never visited before — were each more picturesque than the last; the serfs everywhere seemed thriving and touchingly grateful for the benefits conferred on them. Everywhere there were receptions, which, though they embarrassed Pierre, stirred a joyful feeling deep in his heart. In one place the peasants presented him with bread, salt, and an icon of Saints Peter and Paul, and asked permission — as a mark of gratitude — to build a new chapel at their own expense in honor of his patron saints. In another, the women with babies came to thank him for releasing them from hard labor. On a third estate, the priest came to meet him bearing a cross, surrounded by children whom — thanks to the count's generosity — he was teaching reading, writing, and religion. On all his estates Pierre saw brick buildings either completed or under construction, all built to the same plan, for hospitals, schools, and almshouses — which were due to open soon. Everywhere he saw the stewards' accounts showing that the serfs' compulsory labor had been reduced, and heard the grateful speeches of deputations of serfs in their best blue coats.

What Pierre did not know was this: the place where they presented him with bread and salt and wanted to build a chapel in honor of Peter and Paul was a market village where a fair was held on Saint Peter's Day, and that the richest peasants (who made up the deputation) had started building the chapel long before; nine-tenths of the peasants in that village were in extreme poverty. He did not know that since the nursing mothers were no longer sent to work on his land, they now did even harder work on their own. He did not know that the priest who met him with the cross was squeezing the peasants for fees, and that the pupils' parents wept at having to give up their children, paying heavily to get them back. He did not know that the brick buildings, built to a uniform plan, were being constructed by serf labor — increasing their workload, even though it had been reduced on paper. He did not know that where the steward's accounts showed a one-third reduction in the serfs' payments, their obligatory estate labor had been increased by half. And so Pierre was delighted with his visit to his estates and wrote enthusiastic letters to his "brother-instructor," as he called the Grand Master.
"How easy it is, how little effort it takes, to do so much good," thought Pierre, "and how little attention we pay to it!"
He was pleased by the gratitude he received but felt awkward about it. The gratitude reminded him of how much more he could do for these simple, kind people.

The chief steward — a very stupid but cunning man who saw right through the naive and intelligent count and played him like a toy — observing the effect of these staged receptions, pressed him even harder with arguments about the impossibility and especially the pointlessness of freeing the serfs, who were perfectly happy as they were.

Pierre secretly agreed with the steward that it would be hard to imagine happier people, and God only knew what would happen to them when they were free — but he insisted, though reluctantly, on what he believed was right. The steward promised to do everything in his power to carry out the count's wishes, knowing perfectly well that not only would the count never check whether the forests had actually been sold or the Land Bank loans paid off, but would probably never even ask — and would never find out that the newly built buildings stood empty and that the serfs continued to hand over, in money and labor, everything that could be squeezed from them.

title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: The assistant led Rostov along the corridor to the officers' wards, which consisted of three rooms with open doors. These rooms had actual beds, and the sick and wounded officers were lying or sitting on them. Some walked about in hospital gowns. The first person Rostov met in the officers' ward was a thin little man with one arm, walking around the first room in a nightcap and hospital gown, a pipe clenched between his teeth. Rostov looked at him, trying to remember where he'd seen him before.
